title: Changing an existing contract
summary: A modification changes duties under an existing contract. Identify the proposed change and the governing law before deciding whether new consideration, good faith, a writing, or assent is required.
notes:
Alaska Packers applies the pre-existing-duty rule to a demand for increased pay for the same work after the workers had reached a remote location. Watkins examines the parties’ response to unexpected excavation conditions and their subsequent agreement. Austin addresses a price increase obtained through a threat to withhold urgently needed goods when practical alternatives were unavailable. These cases ask different questions: whether an exchange supports the change, whether the agreement was genuinely voluntary, and whether an asserted adjustment responds fairly to circumstances.

UCC § 2-209 removes a new-consideration requirement for a covered modification, while the assigned discussion retains limits involving good faith, form, and assent. A no-oral-modification clause raises another inquiry; a failed modification may have consequences as a waiver. The New York signed-writing provision in the supplement supplies a separate statutory route. Keep those routes distinct rather than treating “both agreed” as the whole analysis.

textbookImport.basis: Plain-language synthesis of the cited casebook passages; subject to the jurisdictional and source limits stated there.

topics.modification: The rules for changing a bargain differ across sources and circumstances.
